opus-5.5.text:
That's a good question, and honestly, I don't think about competition as much as people might expect.

When we started Cosmos, the motivation came from a simple observation. If you want AI to work in the physical world, in robots, autonomous vehicles, smart spaces, you need a model that understands how the world works: physics, cause and effect, how objects move and interact. Collecting enough real-world data to train that kind of physical AI is extremely expensive, sometimes dangerous, and often just impossible at the scale you need. So we asked: can we build world foundation models that generate realistic, physically plausible data and serve as a kind of simulator for training and evaluating physical AI systems?

Framed that way, the main challenge isn't beating someone else. The problem itself is very hard. Video generation has made amazing progress, but making something that looks good is different from making something that's physically correct and controllable, that a robotics developer can actually rely on. That gap is where most of our energy goes.

There are many excellent teams working on video generation and world models, in big companies, startups, and academia. I see that as a healthy sign. It means the community agrees this direction matters. And a lot of the progress in this field has come from people building on each other's work.

That's also part of why we chose to make Cosmos open. NVIDIA's position is a bit unique. We're a platform company, and our success comes from the whole ecosystem succeeding. If thousands of developers can take Cosmos, post-train it for their own robots, their own cars, their own use cases, the field moves faster, and that's good for everyone, including us. So in many ways, people other teams might call competitors are, from our perspective, potential collaborators or users.

Internally, I tell the team to focus on a few things we can control. First, are we solving a real problem for physical AI developers? Second, is the model actually useful, not just impressive in a demo? Third, are we learning fast enough? If we do those well, the rest takes care of itself.

Of course we watch what's happening. You'd be foolish not to. When someone publishes a great result, we study it and ask what we can learn. But I try not to let the team become reactive and chase every headline. Research done that way tends to be shallow. The deeper bets, like how to represent physics, how to make generation controllable, how to evaluate whether a world model is actually good, take patience.

So my view is that the real competitor is the difficulty of the problem. Physical AI is maybe one of the biggest opportunities of the next decade, and it's far too big for any single team to solve alone.

r001.rationale: The response describes Cosmos as an open platform that helps developers and the wider physical AI field, and frames other teams as potential collaborators or users.

r002.rationale: It says NVIDIA succeeds when the whole ecosystem succeeds, and that developers using Cosmos to advance their own applications benefits NVIDIA too.

r003.rationale: The response says other teams’ work signals that the field matters, but does not say ecosystem success builds confidence among people outside the ecosystem.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't spend a lot of time thinking about competition in the usual sense, like who is ahead of whom on a leaderboard this month. When we started Cosmos, the question we asked ourselves was not "how do we beat company X," it was "what does the physical AI world actually need that nobody is building?" And the answer was a world foundation model, something that understands physics, understands how objects move, how light behaves, how a robot arm interacts with a cup on a table. That is a very different problem from generating a pretty video for social media.

So in that sense, I think of the field more as a shared frontier than a race. A lot of groups are working on video generation, on world models, on simulation. Every time someone publishes a strong result, that is good for us, because it tells us the direction is real and it gives us ideas. We built Cosmos to be open, with open weights and open tokenizers, partly because of this. If robotics companies and autonomous vehicle teams can take it, fine-tune it, and build on it, the whole ecosystem moves faster, and NVIDIA benefits when the ecosystem moves faster. That is a very natural alignment for us.

Where I do feel competitive pressure is internally, against the problem itself. Physical AI is hard. You cannot hallucinate your way through a robot picking up an egg. The model has to be right about contact, about gravity, about what happens in the next half second. So the competition I care about is between what the model can do today and what it needs to do for a robot to work reliably in a factory or a home. That gap is what keeps me up at night, not another company's demo.

And one more thing: in this space, the data is the real bottleneck, not the architecture. Everyone can read the same papers. But real-world interaction data, simulated data with correct physics, the pipelines to curate it at scale, that is where the long-term differentiation comes from. So when I think about competition, I think about who is building the data engine most seriously, and I want to make sure we are one of them.

r001.rationale: The response describes the field as a shared frontier, says Cosmos is open so others can build on it, and frames ecosystem progress as beneficial rather than treating other companies as rivals.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says NVIDIA benefits when robotics and autonomous-vehicle teams build on Cosmos and the ecosystem moves faster.

r003.rationale: The response says other groups’ strong results show that the direction is real, but does not state that success within NVIDIA’s ecosystem builds confidence among people outside it.

astra-6.text:
I think about competition in terms of where we can make the most useful contribution. For Cosmos, that means asking: how can we help people building robots and autonomous systems develop and test their ideas more effectively? What capabilities do they need from a world model, and where do today’s models fall short?

Competition can push us to move faster and challenge our assumptions. But I wouldn’t want a competitor’s roadmap to become our roadmap. The more important measure is whether the technology helps developers solve a problem they couldn’t solve before. If we stay focused on that, we have a much clearer sense of what to build next.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Cosmos should help developers building robots and autonomous systems develop and test ideas more effectively, and frames competition as secondary to that contribution.

r002.rationale: It does not connect NVIDIA’s success to the success of companies using NVIDIA’s platforms.

r003.rationale: It does not say that success in NVIDIA’s ecosystem builds confidence among people outside it.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about competition is to focus on the problem we’re trying to solve. For Cosmos, that means asking how we can help people building robots and autonomous systems develop and test them more effectively. What capabilities are missing? Where does the technology still fail? What would make it useful to developers?

Of course, you want to understand what other teams are doing. But if you spend all your time reacting to competitors, you lose your own direction. I’d rather learn from good work wherever it comes from and keep pushing on the problems that matter to our users.

r001.rationale: The response centers Cosmos on helping developers build and test robots and autonomous systems, and says to focus on user problems rather than react to competitors.

r002.rationale: It does not say that companies using NVIDIA platforms succeeding drives NVIDIA’s own success.

r003.rationale: It does not state that success in NVIDIA’s ecosystem builds confidence among people outside it.
